title: Loop back: everything you can do now
idea: LOOP (review), capstone. A broad sweep across Laps 0-5 and the decomposition/debugging habits, closing the lap before combining techniques.

exercises.prompt: Match each lap to a core thing it gave you.

pairs.right: Remember values and compute a result

exercises.explanation: Six laps, six capabilities. Together they are the toolkit you now break big problems down with.

exercises.prompt: What is the first step whenever you face a bigger problem?
options: Understand it: name the inputs and the output
exercises.explanation: Understand first — inputs and output — then example, plan, code, check. The flow that steadies every solve.

exercises.prompt: Working one example by hand gives you the answer to check your code against later.
exercises.explanation: Yes. The hand example is your measuring stick — it is how Check knows whether the code is right.

exercises.prompt: You split a problem into helpers and the answer is wrong. What do you do?
options: Test each helper against a known value to localize the bug, then check the wiring
exercises.explanation: Localize: clear the good parts, corner the bad one; if all parts are right, suspect the wiring. The debugging habit from Unit 81.

exercises.prompt: Which builtins does this course deliberately avoid, computing them by hand instead?
exercises.explanation: We build totals, biggests, and smallests by hand with loops. (len is allowed, for the size of a list.)

exercises.prompt: A helper that averages a list must guard which input?
options: The empty list, to avoid dividing by zero
exercises.explanation: Dividing by the count breaks on an empty list. The edge-case habit says: enumerate it, then guard it.

exercises.prompt: Order the UEPCC flow you have used all lap.
blocks: Plan the ordered steps and pick patterns
Write the code for the plan
Check the output against the example, then re-run with new inputs
exercises.explanation: Understand, Example, Plan, Code, Check. This is the backbone of every guided solve in the course.

exercises.prompt: Why break a big problem into small helpers at all?
options: Each part is easy to write, easy to test, and easy to fix on its own
It makes the program longer for no reason
exercises.explanation: Small parts are understandable and checkable. Decomposition turns a scary problem into a handful of simple ones.

exercises.prompt: Re-running a finished solution with fresh inputs helps prove it works for more than the first example.
exercises.explanation: Yes — the Check habit. A solution that only works on one example may hide a bug; new inputs build confidence.

exercises.prompt: You are about to start Lap 6 (combining techniques). What have Laps 0-5 prepared you to do?
options: Break a bigger problem into parts, solve each with a known pattern, compose and debug the result
exercises.explanation: You can decompose, pick patterns, compose helpers, handle edges, and debug a split solution. Next: combining several patterns in one problem.
